title: Citizens to Preserve Overton Park, Inc. v. Volpe (1971)
shortTitle: Citizens to Preserve Overton Park, Inc. v. Volpe (1971)
summary: Review of an informal highway approval required the actual administrative record and a searching inquiry within a narrow standard of review.
notes:
Justice Marshall wrote for the Court (Douglas took no part; Black, joined by Brennan, and Blackmun concurred separately); the opinion reads APA § 701(a)(2)'s commitment-to-discretion exception as a narrow one reserved for cases in which there is 'no law to apply,' and describes arbitrary-and-capricious review as a searching and careful inquiry that is nevertheless narrow and does not let the court substitute its judgment for the agency's.

The statutes were § 4(f) of the Department of Transportation Act of 1966 and § 138 of the Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1968, and the highway was Interstate 40 through Overton Park in Memphis, Tennessee; the case is often cited as the starting point of public-interest environmental litigation.

sections.Parties: Private citizens and conservation organizations challenged the Secretary of Transportation’s approval of federal funds for a six-lane interstate highway through Overton Park in Memphis.
sections.Material Facts: The governing statutes prohibited funding a highway through protected parkland when a feasible and prudent alternative existed and otherwise required all possible planning to minimize harm. The challengers maintained that routes north or south were available, that harm could be reduced, and that the Secretary had relied on local officials without making his own determination. The Secretary defended his authority and asserted that he had independently assessed the relevant facts.
sections.Procedural History: The district court reviewed affidavits prepared for litigation, declined requested discovery, and sustained the approval; the court of appeals affirmed. The Supreme Court reversed and remanded for review based on the full administrative record before the Secretary, with further explanation if necessary.
sections.Issue: Was the approval reviewable, which standard applied, and could litigation affidavits substitute for examination of the agency’s contemporaneous record and reasoning?
sections.Holding: The approval was reviewable under the APA, and arbitrary-and-capricious review applied. Neither substantial-evidence review nor de novo factfinding governed this informal approval. Formal findings were not independently required by the relevant statutes, but the affidavits did not provide an adequate basis for review.
sections.Reasoning: The statutory conditions supplied law to apply, defeating the claim that the decision was wholly committed to agency discretion. Congress gave preservation of parkland paramount importance; ordinary cost and displacement considerations could not automatically justify using a park, because that would drain the protection of effect. A court must determine the agency’s authority, whether it considered relevant factors and avoided a clear error of judgment, and whether it followed required procedure. The inquiry is searching, while the court’s authority to substitute its policy judgment remains narrow. Review must use the actual record, not counsel’s post hoc justification. Because there were no contemporaneous formal findings, the Court allowed the district court to seek an explanation and possibly testimony, while warning that inquiries into decisionmakers’ mental processes are ordinarily avoided. Where contemporaneous findings exist, a strong showing of bad faith or improper behavior is necessary for that kind of inquiry. The remand did not itself decide that every alternative route was feasible or order construction on a particular route.

topics.lrs-n-hard-look: The court required searching consideration of relevant factors while preserving the agency’s role in making the ultimate choice.
topics.lrs-n-administrative-record: Review had to use the full contemporaneous administrative record rather than affidavits constructed for litigation.
topics.lrs-n-nonreviewability: The park-protection statute supplied meaningful standards and therefore law to apply.
topics.lrs-o-chenery-reasons: The Court refused to review the approval on litigation affidavits and required the contemporaneous administrative record, the same anti-post-hoc-rationalization principle as Chenery.
